stories.title: Renovation Firm Investigated After Customers Left in a Fix
stories.headline_kid: Police are investigating a home renovation company after many customers said their homes were left half-finished and their furniture went missing.
summary: A Singapore interior design company called Axion Design is now being investigated by the police. Many customers paid the company to renovate their homes, but the work stopped halfway, and some furniture they ordered never arrived.
Some families say they are owed tens of thousands of dollars. Others had to keep living in homes with unfinished floors, kitchens or cupboards, which must have been very stressful and inconvenient.

The police probe means officers are now collecting evidence and speaking to affected customers to find out exactly what went wrong. This is a serious matter because so much money and trust was involved.

This story is a good reminder that before paying a large amount of money for any service, families should check a company's reputation carefully — just like how you'd check reviews before choosing a stall for your favourite snack.

lenses.me: If your family is planning to renovate your home one day, this story shows why it's smart to check a company carefully before paying them.
lenses.family: Parents may feel more cautious about giving large deposits to renovation firms before the work is actually done.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose families are renovating their flats might talk about delays or problems at home.
lenses.nation: Singapore's authorities step in to protect consumers when businesses fail to keep their promises, which helps keep trust in local companies strong.
lenses.world: This shows why consumer protection rules matter everywhere, whenever people pay in advance for a service.

compo_words.example: The renovation works stalled for months, leaving the family without a proper kitchen.

stories.title: Should Singapore's Leaders Earn More If They Do a Better Job?
stories.headline_kid: Grown-ups are debating whether Singapore's government ministers should be paid more, but only if they perform really well at their jobs.
summary: Ministers are a bit like the people in charge of running Singapore — they make big decisions about things like schools, hospitals and transport. A veteran editor has written that ministers could be paid more, but their pay should be linked to how well they perform.

This is similar to how some jobs give workers a bonus only if they do a great job, like getting extra pocket money for finishing all your homework well and on time. The idea is that this could encourage leaders to work extra hard and be more accountable.

But it's not simple. Some people think it's hard to measure exactly how 'well' a minister has done, since running a country isn't like a test with a clear score. Others feel this could help attract capable, hardworking people to serve in government, especially since good leaders are in demand everywhere.
This is still just a discussion for now — no decision has been made. But it shows how Singapore keeps thinking about fair ways to reward its leaders.

lenses.me: You may hear grown-ups discuss this on the news, and it helps you understand how our country's leaders are paid and why fairness matters.
lenses.family: Parents pay taxes that help fund government salaries, so how ministers are paid can indirectly affect family finances.
lenses.friends: Friends might bring this up if they've heard their parents talking about it at home or on the news.
lenses.nation: Singapore wants to attract and keep capable leaders, and this debate is about how best to reward good leadership.
lenses.world: Many countries face similar debates about how much to pay their leaders and how to measure good leadership fairly.

compo_words.example: The company reviewed each worker's performance before deciding on bonuses.

stories.title: Oil Prices Jump After Attacks Near the Persian Gulf
stories.headline_kid: Oil got a lot more expensive over the weekend after attacks near Saudi Arabia and an important sea passage — and this could make things pricier in Singapore too.
summary: Over the weekend, there were new attacks on Saudi Arabia and on ships near the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow sea passage where huge oil tankers travel, a bit like a busy expressway just for oil ships. Because of this, people worried the oil supply might be disrupted, so oil prices jumped by more than US$3 in a single day.

Singapore doesn't produce its own oil — we import all of it from other countries. So when oil becomes pricier around the world, things like petrol, cooking gas, and even bus or taxi fares can slowly become more expensive too. It's a bit like how your favourite snack costs more if its ingredients suddenly become expensive.

This latest price jump is linked to ongoing tension in the Middle East, involving countries like Saudi Arabia and a group called the Houthis in Yemen. It's a complicated, faraway conflict, but its effects can reach all the way to Singapore through oil prices.

Stock markets across Asia also dipped as investors grew nervous, and some are watching to see if central banks like the US Federal Reserve might raise interest rates this week, which can make borrowing money more costly.

lenses.me: If oil prices stay high, your family may notice petrol and transport costs creeping up slowly.
lenses.family: Parents who drive or take cabs might find fares slightly pricier because fuel now costs more.
lenses.friends: Friends who take buses to school won't feel much difference, but family outings by car could cost a bit more.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports all its oil, so swings in global oil prices directly affect our economy and cost of living.
lenses.world: Many countries depend on oil passing through the Middle East, so instability there raises prices for everyone.

compo_words.example: Oil prices experienced a surge after the attacks.

compo_words.example: The strikes threatened to disrupt oil supplies from the region.

compo_words.example: Global oil prices have become increasingly volatile amid the conflict.

compo_phrases.example: The attacks caused a ripple effect on oil prices worldwide.

compo_phrases.meaning: to spend money carefully and cut back on spending
compo_phrases.example: Families may need to tighten their belts if fuel prices keep rising.

stories.title: Ferry Capsizes Off Indonesia, Over 120 People Missing
stories.headline_kid: A ferry carrying many passengers capsized near Indonesia, and rescuers are racing to find more than 120 people still missing.
summary: A ferry called Virgo Transport 8 capsized, meaning it flipped over in the water, off the coast of Indonesia near Java and Kalimantan. So far, six people are confirmed to have died, and 129 others are still missing, while 108 passengers have been rescued.

Indonesia's search and rescue teams, called Basarnas, are working hard using boats and divers to look for survivors and those still missing. Families of the passengers are anxiously waiting by the shore for news of their loved ones.

Indonesia is Singapore's close neighbour, and many Singaporean families travel there by ferry, for example to islands like Batam or Bintan, for short holidays. This sad event reminds everyone how important it is for ferries to follow strict safety rules, like having enough life jackets for every passenger.
Singapore, as a major seaport itself, often works closely with neighbouring countries on maritime safety and rescue efforts, since keeping the seas safe matters to the whole region.

lenses.me: This story reminds you why wearing a life jacket and following safety rules on boats is so important.
lenses.family: If your family travels by ferry to nearby islands like Batam or Bintan, this news might make parents extra careful about checking safety measures.
lenses.friends: Classmates who have been on ferry trips with family can relate to how serious ferry safety really is.
lenses.nation: Singapore, as a major seaport, works closely with Indonesia on maritime safety and rescue cooperation.
lenses.world: This tragedy highlights why strict safety checks for ferries and ships matter everywhere, not just in one country.

compo_words.meaning: when a boat turns over in the water
compo_words.example: The ferry capsized suddenly during rough weather.

compo_phrases.meaning: to hurry to do something before it's too late
compo_phrases.example: Rescuers are in a race against time to find survivors.

stories.title: Popular Singapore Bakery Baker's Brew Closes For Good
stories.headline_kid: Baker's Brew, a well-loved Singapore bakery many families visited for birthday cakes, has shut down after running into money troubles.
summary: Baker's Brew Studio was a homegrown Singapore bakery with outlets at places like Great World City, Paragon, Upper Thomson and JEM. Last year, it changed its name to BB Atelier.

Now, the company has gone into liquidation. This means it owes more money than it can pay back, so it must close down and sort out its debts with the help of appointed liquidators — a bit like when someone can't finish a big project and needs help to tidy everything up.

The good news is that about 95% of affected customers have already gotten their money back, for example those who had bought vouchers or store credit in advance. Its last physical outlet at Great World City closed back in June.

Many Singaporean families may have fond memories of buying birthday cakes or pastries from this bakery over the years. This story is a gentle reminder that even well-known, beloved businesses can face hard times and eventually close.

lenses.family: Parents who had store credit or vouchers with the bakery would want to check if they've received their refunds.
lenses.friends: Classmates might share memories of birthday parties with cakes from this bakery.
lenses.nation: This shows how even well-known Singapore businesses can struggle financially and eventually have to close.
lenses.world: It's a reminder that running a business is hard everywhere, and companies must manage their money carefully to survive.
